# Routeveil: complete AI-readable reference

## Product identity

Routeveil is an open-source React and TypeScript transition engine for React Router.
It coordinates page animations, full-screen overlay effects, shared elements, route
readiness, scroll, focus, and cleanup around individual navigation requests.

Routeveil does not replace React Router. React Router owns routing, history, location,
and route rendering. Routeveil owns the temporary visual lifecycle around an explicitly
transitioned navigation.

Canonical sources:

- Website: https://www.routeveil.dev/
- Documentation: https://www.routeveil.dev/docs
- Releases: https://www.routeveil.dev/releases
- Interactive transition lab: https://www.routeveil.dev/lab
- Between-render lab: https://www.routeveil.dev/lab/between
- Shared-elements playground: https://www.routeveil.dev/lab/shared-elements
- Source: https://github.com/milkevich/routeveil
- npm: https://www.npmjs.com/package/routeveil

The package name is `routeveil`. Import runtime APIs from
`routeveil/react-router`. The package root is not a runtime entry point. Routeveil is
licensed under the MIT License.

## Release history

- `0.4.1` (2026-08-08) — Shared Element Stability: Shared element transitions are now significantly more reliable and responsive across mobile browsers, complex scrolling layouts, and layered sticky or fixed interface elements.
- `0.4.0` (2026-08-02) — Between Rendering: Routeveil can now render controlled React content between route exit and entry, with readiness holds, minimum timing, and same-page playback.
- `0.3.1` (2026-07-31) — Transition Request Guard: Rapid repeated activations now reuse the active transition instead of restarting visual work or committing duplicate navigation.
- `0.3.0` (2026-07-31) — Unified Transition API: A redesigned transition input unifies names, options, and independent page phases under one fully typed API.
- `0.2.5` (2026-07-28) — Provider Lifecycle Refinements: Provider internals, shared-element coordination, and transition cleanup were refined for more efficient and dependable navigation.
- `0.2.4` (2026-07-27) — Snapshot Pipeline: A new viewport snapshot pipeline made page transitions more visually stable while improving shared elements, preloading, and mobile performance.
- `0.2.3` (2026-07-26) — Shared Element Matching: Shared movement now begins only when Routeveil confirms that a valid matching element exists on the destination route.
- `0.2.2` (2026-07-25) — Route-wide Shared Elements: Shared-element navigation can now be triggered by controls outside the element being moved.
- `0.2.1` (2026-07-25) — Preloading and Route Readiness: Routes and their visual dependencies can now be prepared before reveal, reducing delays between navigation and the incoming transition.
- `0.2.0` (2026-07-25) — Shared Element Transitions: Routeveil gained coordinated visual movement between matching elements on outgoing and incoming React Router routes.
- `0.1.1` (2026-07-22) — Production Readiness: This release strengthened Routeveil’s package output, documentation, metadata, deployment setup, and browser behavior after the initial launch.
- `0.1.0` (2026-07-21) — Core Transition Engine: Routeveil’s first public build established its typed page and full-screen overlay transition engine for React Router.

## Installation and compatibility

```bash
npm install routeveil
```

Peer dependencies:

- React: `^18.0.0 || ^19.0.0`
- React DOM: `^18.0.0 || ^19.0.0`
- React Router DOM: `^6.27.0 || ^7.0.0`

React Router 5 and React Router 8 are not supported by the current adapter. TypeScript
declarations are included. The library is distributed as an ES module.

The packed-package verification matrix is:

| React | React DOM | React Router DOM |
| --- | --- | --- |
| React 18.0.0 | React DOM 18.0.0 | React Router DOM 6.27.0 |
| React 18.3.1 | React DOM 18.3.1 | React Router DOM 6.30.4 |
| React 19.0.0 | React DOM 19.0.0 | React Router DOM 6.27.0 |
| React 19.2.8 | React DOM 19.2.8 | React Router DOM 6.30.4 |
| React 18.0.0 | React DOM 18.0.0 | React Router DOM 7.0.0 |
| React 18.3.1 | React DOM 18.3.1 | React Router DOM 7.18.1 |
| React 19.0.0 | React DOM 19.0.0 | React Router DOM 7.0.0 |
| React 19.2.8 | React DOM 19.2.8 | React Router DOM 7.18.1 |
| React 19.2.7 | React DOM 19.2.7 | React Router DOM 7.18.1 |

Each fixture validates installation, dependency identity, public imports, TypeScript,
runtime navigation, and a production build. React Router DOM versions below 6.27.0
and untested combinations are unsupported.

```ts
import {
  RouteveilBetween,
  RouteveilLink,
  RouteveilProvider,
  RouteveilSharedElement,
  RouteveilView,
  useRouteveilNavigate,
  useRouteveilPendingWork,
  useRouteveilTransition,
} from 'routeveil/react-router'
```

## Minimal setup

`RouteveilProvider` must render beneath React Router context. One active
`RouteveilView` marks the route region animated by page transitions.

```tsx
<BrowserRouter>
  <RouteveilProvider>
    <Header />
    <RouteveilView>
      <Routes>
        <Route path="/" element={<Home />} />
        <Route path="/about" element={<About />} />
      </Routes>
    </RouteveilView>
  </RouteveilProvider>
</BrowserRouter>
```

Persistent UI stays mounted when placed outside `RouteveilView`. In a Data Router
layout, an empty `RouteveilView` renders React Router's `Outlet`.

## Unified transition input

`RouteveilLink`, `useRouteveilNavigate`, and `useRouteveilTransition` accept the
same `RouteveilTransition` value.

### Complete shorthand

```ts
transition: 'fade'
```

A page name uses both the definition's exit and enter phases. An overlay name uses its
cover and reveal lifecycle.

### Configured complete transition

```ts
transition: {
  name: 'slide',
  direction: 'left',
}
```

Options are flattened beside `name`. There is no nested `options` property. The
resolver receives the flattened options with the structural `name` field removed.

Overlay configuration uses the same shape:

```ts
transition: {
  name: 'tunnel',
  origin: 'cursor',
  color: '#111111',
}
```

### Split page transition

```ts
transition: {
  exit: 'fade',
  enter: {
    name: 'slide',
    direction: 'up',
  },
}
```

`exit` and `enter` resolve independently. Routeveil uses only the selected
definition's exit phase for `exit` and only its enter phase for `enter`. Options are
not shared between phases.

Each phase accepts a name or a configured object:

```ts
transition: {
  exit: {
    name: 'slide',
    direction: 'left',
  },
  enter: {
    name: 'slide',
    direction: 'right',
  },
}
```

Split transitions accept page definitions only. Overlay names are invalid in
`exit` and `enter`.

At least one phase is required. An omitted phase is absent:

```ts
transition: { exit: 'fade' }
transition: { enter: 'slide' }
```

Routeveil does not copy the other phase, choose a default, reuse an opposite phase, or
create a zero-duration animation.

### Runtime fallback

Unknown names, invalid split overlay phases, and resolver errors do not trap the
application. A valid split phase still runs when the other phase is invalid. If no
valid phase remains, navigation completes without animation. Cleanup removes all
Routeveil-owned snapshots, backgrounds, between and overlay layers, timers, animations,
inert state, temporary attributes, and pending lifecycle state.

## Page transition lifecycle

The normal sequence is:

1. prepare and animate the outgoing `RouteveilView`
2. commit React Router navigation
3. wait for the incoming location, browser paints, and registered pending work
4. apply scroll and shared-element behavior
5. animate the incoming `RouteveilView`
6. restore visibility, interaction, focus, overflow, backgrounds, and idle state

With no exit phase, Routeveil skips outgoing page animation and its related snapshot,
retained-background animation, watchdog, and timer work. Without a navigation-level
between fallback, the current page remains visible while an unfinished preload settles.
With a fallback, Routeveil suppresses the outgoing view, shows between content, then
commits when preload permits. Content supplied only by the incoming route appears after
commit.

With no enter phase, Routeveil completes exit, navigation, readiness, scrolling, and
whichever visual handoff applies. Active between content disappears before Routeveil
reveals the incoming route without a page enter animation.

A missing page phase does not disable shared-element movement.

With navigation-level between content, the page lifecycle is
`exit → between → navigate and prepare → enter`:

1. run page exit
2. show the fallback with the exit definition's complementary enter motion
3. commit navigation and wait for the incoming route
4. crossfade to the newest incoming `RouteveilBetween` content, when registered
5. wait for readiness, every active hold, and minimum timing
6. animate and remove between content with the enter definition's complementary exit motion
7. run page enter

With only incoming `RouteveilBetween`, navigation happens first. The registration then
shows between content before enter or reveal. Content controls its own height and
alignment; it does not inherit the incoming page's height.

## Overlay transition lifecycle

The sequence is:

1. mount and prepare the overlay through a `document.body` portal
2. cover the complete viewport
3. commit navigation after the old screen is hidden
4. wait for the incoming route
5. reveal the destination
6. reset and remove the overlay

With navigation-level between content, the overlay lifecycle is
`cover → between → navigate and prepare → reveal`. With only incoming
`RouteveilBetween`, navigation happens first; between content then appears before
reveal. Cover completes before between content appears, and reveal starts after it
disappears.

Configured overlay options are passed to the renderer. A clicked
`RouteveilLink` supplies pointer coordinates. Keyboard and programmatic navigation use
the center fallback. Playback may explicitly pass `clickPosition`.

## Core components

### RouteveilProvider

Owns the transition registry and lifecycle. Props:

- `children: ReactNode`
- `transitions?: Record<string, TransitionDefinition>`
- `preload?: false | 'intent' | 'viewport' | 'render'`

Built-ins are automatic. Custom definitions extend the registry. A custom definition
with a built-in name replaces that built-in inside the provider.

There is no provider-level default transition. Each request supplies
`transition` or navigates normally.

### RouteveilView

Registers the one stable routed wrapper animated by page effects. Props:

- `children?: ReactNode`, defaulting to `Outlet`
- `className?: string`
- `style?: CSSProperties`

The view becomes inert during page transitions and exposes Routeveil phase and busy
state. While between content is active, it exposes
`data-routeveil-phase="between"`. Cleanup restores its previous state.

### RouteveilBetween

Registers incoming-route content for the active between phase. Props:

- `content: ReactNode`
- `while?: boolean`, defaulting to `false`
- `minDuration?: number`, defaulting to `0`

`content` is required; there is no `children` alternative. A true `while` value holds
enter or reveal until it becomes false or the registration unmounts. `minDuration` is a
minimum number of milliseconds from between appearance start, not an exact deadline.
Invalid, negative, and non-finite durations normalize to `0`.

### RouteveilLink

Extends React Router's `Link`. Routeveil additions:

- `transition?: RouteveilTransition`
- `between?: RouteveilBetweenInput`
- `preload?: false | 'intent' | 'viewport' | 'render'`
- `smoothScrollToTop?: boolean`
- `scrollToSharedElement?: string`
- `sharedElements?: 'auto' | 'all' | string | readonly string[] | false`

Routeveil calls the consumer `onClick` first and respects `preventDefault`.
External URLs, downloads, `reloadDocument`, non-self targets, modified clicks,
non-primary clicks, prevented events, and same-location links preserve native behavior.
A selected Routeveil transition owns the visual lifecycle instead of React Router's
native `viewTransition` option.

### RouteveilSharedElement

Accepts `name: string` and one React element child. It adds no layout wrapper; it
clones the child with a merged ref. Custom components must forward their ref to one HTML
or SVG element. Names must be unique within one active route view.

## Hooks

### useRouteveilNavigate

Performs programmatic transition-aware navigation. It accepts React Router
`NavigateOptions` plus `transition`, `between`, `smoothScrollToTop`,
`scrollToSharedElement`, and `sharedElements`.

Its promise resolves after the visual lifecycle and cleanup. Without `transition`,
or when pathname, search, and hash are unchanged, it delegates without a Routeveil
animation.

### useRouteveilTransition

Plays a page or overlay transition on the current route without navigating, changing
URL, adding history, changing location state, remounting the route, or moving scroll.
Its promise resolves after animation and cleanup. Playback supports `between` content
and `minDuration`.

The optional second argument is:

```ts
{
  between?: RouteveilBetweenInput
  clickPosition?: {
    x: number
    y: number
  }
}
```

### useRouteveilPendingWork

Returns a registrar for asynchronous incoming-route work:

```ts
const release = registerPendingWork(promise)
```

Register work during an active destination readiness window when an incoming visual
must settle before enter or reveal. The returned function releases the task early,
typically during effect cleanup. Rejection counts as settled. A safety timeout prevents
indefinite blocking. `<RouteveilBetween>`'s `while` prop adds a separate hold; both systems must
release before enter or reveal.

## Between rendering

`RouteveilLink`, `useRouteveilNavigate`, and `useRouteveilTransition` can provide
immediate between content in either form:

```tsx
<RouteveilLink
  to="/dashboard"
  transition="fade"
  between={<BrandLogo />}
>
  Dashboard
</RouteveilLink>

navigate('/dashboard', {
  transition: 'fade',
  between: {
    content: <BrandLogo />,
    minDuration: 500,
  },
})
```

The incoming route can take control without losing its React context, state, or hooks:

```tsx
<RouteveilBetween
  content={<LoadingStatus />}
  while={isLoading}
  minDuration={500}
/>
```

The provider owns the visual layer. Each incoming component portals its live content
into that layer while remaining in its original React tree. When supplied, the
navigation fallback is visible first. The newest active incoming registration replaces
it with a crossfade; if that registration unmounts, Routeveil falls back through older
incoming registrations and finally to the navigation fallback.

All active incoming registrations contribute holds and minimum durations even though
only the newest supplies visible content. Their minimums share the original between
start time, so content replacement does not restart the lifecycle clock. Registrations
are matched to the committed location, preventing stale outgoing content from joining
the run.

Visible-content replacement crossfades without restarting the lifecycle or its minimum
duration clock. Disappearance waits for appearance, route readiness, pending work,
every active hold, and the longest applicable minimum duration.

Routeveil does not impose visual layout on between content. Content controls its own
height and alignment and is not automatically centered or fullscreen. Page between
content does not inherit the incoming page's height. Application CSS can use
`min-height: 100vh` for an intentional fullscreen visual; overlay content may likewise
cover the viewport through user styles. The overlay between layer locks viewport scrolling while
active. Content does not receive pointer interaction.

Page between content appears using the outgoing transition and disappears using the
incoming transition. Routeveil uses each transition's complementary phase. Split phases
resolve independently. If a page phase is omitted, its page animation is absent and the
corresponding between motion uses the layer's standard opacity fallback. Overlays retain
cover and reveal while the overlay between layer handles appearance and disappearance.

Shared movement and between rendering are mutually exclusive. Navigation-level between
content disables shared movement. If shared movement has already started, Routeveil
skips a later incoming between layer.

Reduced motion skips Routeveil motion while preserving content, scope, holds, minimum
timing, readiness, and cleanup.

Supplying `between` without `transition` performs normal React Router navigation and
does not create a between phase. There are no provider defaults, public fade controls,
or source-level holds. Playback supports both between input forms.

## Shared elements

Shared elements compose with page transitions. They are not transition names.

Shared-element movement may start with a short lead and overlap page exit when incoming
preparation finishes early enough. Otherwise movement runs after exit. Without an exit
phase, movement finishes before page enter. Page enter always waits for movement.

Shared movement and between rendering are mutually exclusive. Navigation-level between
content disables shared movement. If shared movement has already started, Routeveil
skips a later incoming between layer.

Source and destination wrappers connect by exact `name`, not tag or tree position.
Routeveil moves a fixed, non-interactive visual clone; it does not move or replace
application DOM. Same-tag visuals can interpolate supported styles. Different tags use
geometry movement and a crossfade.

With `sharedElements='auto'`, a clicked link selects shared elements on, inside, or
around its anchor. Programmatic requests use `scrollToSharedElement` as a source hint,
then the sole available source when unambiguous. Use `all`, exact names, an array, or
`false` for explicit selection.

Multiple unique names move concurrently. Missing, duplicate, or unmeasurable matches
are skipped safely. Overlay transitions and same-page playback ignore shared
registrations. Reduced motion skips clones and movement.

## Route preloading

Preloading applies to eligible internal transitioned `RouteveilLink` destinations:

- `intent`: focus, pointer intent, press, or touch
- `viewport`: link enters the viewport
- `render`: link mounts
- `false`: disabled

A link value overrides the provider default. Automatic discovery requires a Data Router
such as `createBrowserRouter`; declarative `BrowserRouter` does not expose a route
tree. Routeveil runs matching `route.lazy` functions and caches their promises. It
does not render the destination, run component effects, or execute loaders.

An active exit may overlap preloading. If there is no usable exit animation and no
navigation-level between fallback, Routeveil keeps the outgoing page visible while
pending preload work settles. A fallback can occupy the between scope while preload is
still pending. Failure or timeout continues navigation safely.

## Scroll precedence

For successful transitioned navigation:

1. URL hash target
2. valid `scrollToSharedElement` destination
3. `preventScrollReset`
4. top reset, smooth when `smoothScrollToTop` is true and instant otherwise

A shared-element anchor centers the target vertically and preserves horizontal scroll
before shared endpoints are measured. Playback and cancelled runs do not scroll.

## Interrupted navigation and concurrency

Routeveil uses ignore-while-active concurrency. One run and one promise may be active.
Another Routeveil link, navigation, or playback request receives the active promise;
its requested destination is ignored without queueing or replacing the run.

Back, Forward, ordinary React Router navigation, plain links, and direct history
changes are external. The latest location wins. Routeveil abandons an uncommitted
destination, cancels owned visual work, and never repeats a commit that already
happened.

Completed, failed, interrupted, timed-out, and unmounted runs clean up owned visual and
lifecycle state. Stale runs cannot later navigate, focus, scroll, or clear state owned
by another run.

## Focus and accessibility

`RouteveilView` is inert during page transitions. Full-screen overlays block pointer
input. Meaningful connected focus moved by application code is preserved after
navigation. Otherwise Routeveil focuses the incoming view with `preventScroll`.
Disconnected outgoing triggers are never focused.

Same-page playback and failed unchanged navigation restore prior focus only when it is
still connected and application code has not moved focus elsewhere.

## Reduced motion

Before each request, Routeveil reads `prefers-reduced-motion`. When reduction is
requested, it skips page, overlay, shared-element, and between motion while
preserving navigation, between content and scope, holds, minimum timing, route readiness,
scroll, focus, cleanup, and promise behavior.

## Built-in page transitions

- `fade`: opacity crossfade; no transition-specific options
- `blur`: blur and opacity; no transition-specific options
- `slide`: `direction: 'up' | 'down' | 'left' | 'right'`
- `spin`: `direction: 'up' | 'down' | 'left' | 'right'`
- `rotate`: `direction: 'left' | 'right'`
- `bounce`: soft depth movement; no transition-specific options
- `push`: outgoing page advances toward the viewer; no transition-specific options
- `pull`: incoming page is drawn forward; no transition-specific options

## Built-in overlay transitions

- `pixel`: `columns`, `rows`, `color`, `origin`, `duration`, `stagger`; origins are `top-left`, `top-right`, `bottom-left`, `bottom-right`, `center`, `random`, or `cursor`
- `curtain`: `color`, `axis: 'horizontal' | 'vertical'`, `duration`, `easing`
- `wipe`: `color`, `direction: 'right' | 'left' | 'down' | 'up'`, `duration`, `easing`
- `columns`: `columns`, `count`, `direction: 'down' | 'up' | 'alternate'`, `order: 'forward' | 'reverse' | 'center'`, `color`, `duration`, `stagger`, `easing`
- `rows`: `rows`, `count`, `direction: 'right' | 'left' | 'alternate'`, `order: 'forward' | 'reverse' | 'center'`, `color`, `duration`, `stagger`, `easing`
- `iris`: `color`, `origin: 'cursor' | 'center'`, `duration`, `easing`
- `halo`: `color`, `origin: 'cursor' | 'center'`, `duration`, `easing`
- `tunnel`: `color`, `origin: 'cursor' | 'center'`, `duration`, `coverDuration`, `revealDuration`, `easing`
- `clock`: `color`, `origin: 'cursor' | 'center'`, `direction: 'clockwise' | 'counterclockwise'`, `startAngle`, `duration`, `easing`
- `venetian`: `color`, `direction: 'horizontal' | 'vertical'`, `count`, `alternate`, `duration`, `stagger`
- `mosaic`: `colors`, `columns`, `rows`, `duration`, `stagger`, `rotation`, `seed`, `origin: 'cursor' | 'center' | 'random'`
- `dissolve`: `color`, `duration`, `grainSize`, `softness`, `seed`

Most overlays accept `color`; `mosaic` accepts `colors`. `RouteveilLink` supplies pointer
coordinates. Keyboard and programmatic navigation use the center fallback. Playback may
explicitly pass `clickPosition`.

## TypeScript

Important public types include:

- `RouteveilTransition`
- `RouteveilBetweenInput`
- `RouteveilBetweenProps`
- `RouteveilPhase`, including `between`
- `TransitionConfig`
- `PageTransitionInput`
- `SplitTransition`
- `TransitionName`
- `RouteveilLinkProps`
- `RouteveilNavigateOptions`
- `RouteveilProviderProps`
- page, overlay, renderer, animation, option, direction, and origin definition types

Transition options are typed according to each built-in name. Custom names remain
supported and custom resolver options are forwarded as flattened fields.

## Current scope

- Direct loads and refreshes do not animate
- Standard React Router `Link` and `navigate` remain unanimated
- Back and Forward remain native and do not independently start transitions
- One active `RouteveilView` is supported per provider
- Unknown transitions and missing views fall back to safe navigation
- Concurrent Routeveil requests use ignore-while-active behavior
- Next.js integration, cloned route trees, and the browser View Transitions API are not included
